regime.classification: The AI-Valuation Unwind Deepens and Concentrates in Japan, While a Sharply Repriced Hawkish Fed Collides With the Widening Iran/Hormuz War — three separate forces, each strong enough to move markets alone, now overlapping.
regime.justification: Japan's Nikkei 225 sank as much as 4.4% intraday, tumbling to roughly 63,896.48 and briefly breaching the 65,000 level for the first time in about a month (previous close 66,835.54) — a sharp deepening from yesterday's already-severe 2.6% drop, driven by renewed AI-spending anxiety after Taiwan Semiconductor lifted its 2026 capex guidance to $60-64bn (from $52-56bn), which investors read as confirmation of just how much capital the AI buildout still requires rather than as the reassuring beat its headline earnings implied. Kioxia plunged near 16%, Advantest and SoftBank each lost around 9%. Critically, South Korea's KOSPI — which plunged more than 7% yesterday — closed today down only 0.46% at 8,051.33, a meaningful stabilization that marks a bifurcation shift: this is now concentrating specifically in Japan rather than remaining a uniform regional rout. On Wall Street Thursday, the S&P 500 fell 0.51% to 7,533.77 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.47% to 25,881.95, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) down almost 4% and Micron, Intel, Lam Research, and AMD all lower; Nasdaq 100 futures were a further 0.3% softer heading into Friday's session. Separately, and on its own track, the Iran/Strait of Hormuz war extended into a sixth consecutive night of US strikes, with Iran calling the Strait an "unbreakable red line"; the conflict's regional footprint widened further today — Qatar said it intercepted a missile attack (loud bangs heard in Doha), Kuwait said it was responding to threats, and sirens activated in Bahrain — even as Brent crude eased marginally to ~$85.00 from Wednesday's four-day rally high of $85.90, and gold held near $3,984-3,986/oz, still short of the psychologically important $4,000 mark despite the war's severity (the same muted safe-haven paradox this report has flagged for over a week). The most consequential development for this report's own open book, however, is on rates: Fed September rate-hike odds have surged from the sub-17% level this report cited as recently as two sessions ago to a range of roughly 44.5%-56% across sources found this session — a genuinely large, if imprecisely pinned-down, hawkish repricing, fueled by Thursday's stronger-than-expected US data (Initial Claims 208K, beating expectations; Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing surging to 41.4, roughly four times consensus) and this morning's improved preliminary University of Michigan sentiment read. The dollar index (DXY) firmed modestly to ~100.78.
regime.executiveSummary: Today separates cleanly into three stories that are only loosely connected. First, the AI-valuation unwind that began spreading regionally earlier this week has now concentrated hard in Japan specifically — Nikkei -4.4% intraday against KOSPI's much smaller -0.46% — which changes the read from "a regional tech rout" to "a Japan-specific valuation reset," and matters directly for this report's currency-strength scoring (Section 4) and its persistent USD/JPY safe-haven anomaly (Section 6). Second, the Iran/Hormuz war keeps widening geographically (Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain all drawn in today) even as oil itself takes a small breather — reinforcing the view that this remains a slow-burn, structurally bullish-for-oil story rather than a single sharp shock. Third, and most consequential for this tracker's active positions: Thursday's stronger US data and today's Michigan improvement have driven a real, multi-source-confirmed repricing of Fed hike odds, sharply undercutting the dovish-surprise thesis behind this report's open Short USD/JPY idea (Section 2/9) — this is treated as the report's top analytical priority this run, alongside re-confirming the AUD/NZD level that was left unresolved in yesterday's report (see below; largely resolved this session, Section 2).

correlationCheck.text: Today's cross-asset picture again reads as Messy, though the specific inconsistency has shifted. A materially sharper Nikkei selloff (-4.4% intraday, deeper than yesterday's -2.6%) would typically be expected to produce some combination of yen safe-haven buying and broad risk-off dollar demand; instead, USD/JPY is essentially flat and the session's dominant currency story is a Fed-driven, broad-based USD firming that has little to do with the equity selloff at all. Meanwhile KOSPI's stabilization (-0.46% today vs. -7%+ yesterday) suggests the equity story itself is narrowing to Japan specifically rather than broadening regionally, which argues against reading today as a classic risk-off session even as Wall Street closed lower Thursday and Nasdaq futures point softer again. Oil's marginal pullback from Wednesday's highs, even as the Iran/Hormuz conflict's regional footprint visibly widened today (Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain), is itself a modest inconsistency — a geopolitically worse day for the war produced a slightly lower, not higher, oil print. Gold's continued failure to clear $4,000 despite all of the above extends the same paradox flagged for over a week.

**Regime classification: The AI-Valuation Unwind Deepens and Concentrates in Japan, While a Sharply Repriced Hawkish Fed Collides With the Widening Iran/Hormuz War — three separate forces, each strong enough to move markets alone, now overlapping.**

Justification: Japan's Nikkei 225 sank as much as 4.4% intraday, tumbling to roughly 63,896.48 and briefly breaching the 65,000 level for the first time in about a month (previous close 66,835.54) — a sharp deepening from yesterday's already-severe 2.6% drop, driven by renewed AI-spending anxiety after Taiwan Semiconductor lifted its 2026 capex guidance to $60-64bn (from $52-56bn), which investors read as confirmation of just how much capital the AI buildout still requires rather than as the reassuring beat its headline earnings implied. Kioxia plunged near 16%, Advantest and SoftBank each lost around 9%. Critically, South Korea's KOSPI — which plunged more than 7% yesterday — closed today down only 0.46% at 8,051.33, a meaningful stabilization that marks a bifurcation shift: this is now concentrating specifically in Japan rather than remaining a uniform regional rout. On Wall Street Thursday, the S&P 500 fell 0.51% to 7,533.77 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.47% to 25,881.95, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) down almost 4% and Micron, Intel, Lam Research, and AMD all lower; Nasdaq 100 futures were a further 0.3% softer heading into Friday's session. Separately, and on its own track, the Iran/Strait of Hormuz war extended into a sixth consecutive night of US strikes, with Iran calling the Strait an "unbreakable red line"; the conflict's regional footprint widened further today — Qatar said it intercepted a missile attack (loud bangs heard in Doha), Kuwait said it was responding to threats, and sirens activated in Bahrain — even as Brent crude eased marginally to ~$85.00 from Wednesday's four-day rally high of $85.90, and gold held near $3,984-3,986/oz, still short of the psychologically important $4,000 mark despite the war's severity (the same muted safe-haven paradox this report has flagged for over a week). The most consequential development for this report's own open book, however, is on rates: Fed September rate-hike odds have surged from the sub-17% level this report cited as recently as two sessions ago to a range of roughly 44.5%-56% across sources found this session — a genuinely large, if imprecisely pinned-down, hawkish repricing, fueled by Thursday's stronger-than-expected US data (Initial Claims 208K, beating expectations; Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing surging to 41.4, roughly four times consensus) and this morning's improved preliminary University of Michigan sentiment read. The dollar index (DXY) firmed modestly to ~100.78.

**Executive Summary:** Today separates cleanly into three stories that are only loosely connected. First, the AI-valuation unwind that began spreading regionally earlier this week has now concentrated hard in Japan specifically — Nikkei -4.4% intraday against KOSPI's much smaller -0.46% — which changes the read from "a regional tech rout" to "a Japan-specific valuation reset," and matters directly for this report's currency-strength scoring (Section 4) and its persistent USD/JPY safe-haven anomaly (Section 6). Second, the Iran/Hormuz war keeps widening geographically (Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain all drawn in today) even as oil itself takes a small breather — reinforcing the view that this remains a slow-burn, structurally bullish-for-oil story rather than a single sharp shock. Third, and most consequential for this tracker's active positions: Thursday's stronger US data and today's Michigan improvement have driven a real, multi-source-confirmed repricing of Fed hike odds, sharply undercutting the dovish-surprise thesis behind this report's open Short USD/JPY idea (Section 2/9) — this is treated as the report's top analytical priority this run, alongside re-confirming the AUD/NZD level that was left unresolved in yesterday's report (see below; largely resolved this session, Section 2).
